# Warehouse Network Automation & Workforce Transition Roadmap
### Board Paper v1.0 — For Decision at Gate 0 Authorization

**Framing note:** This is the same house style (tag discipline, gated structure, pre-stated flip criteria, cost-to-core rule, visible assumption register) applied to a new and unrelated decision. No substance is carried over from any prior engagement; every figure below originates here and is tagged accordingly.

**Reading conventions**

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **[V]** | Load-bearing claim we have **not** established. Must be verified before any capital is committed. Named owner and gate. |
| **[R]** | Reasoned estimate from industry pattern or arithmetic, **not** our data. Illustrative. Ranges, not points. |
| **[D]** | A decision or design choice we are making. A choice, not a fact. Reversible unless stated. |

Site labels (Site 1–5) are archetypes to be mapped to real facilities at Gate 0. All headcount and dollar figures are **illustrative placeholders** carried at the ranges an operation of this description typically shows [R]; they exist to make the logic auditable, not to be believed.

---

## 1. Recommendation

**Do not buy the vendor's proposal. Split the problem in two, fix the account-damaging errors immediately with near-zero capital, and buy automation slowly, in a modular form, at the sites where it is cheapest to be wrong.**

Specifically:

1. **[D] Treat error rates and labor cost as two separate problems with two separate solutions.** Error rates are a process-and-verification problem solvable network-wide in 4–7 months for low single-digit millions or less [R]. Labor cost is the only legitimate case for capital automation. Buying goods-to-person to fix errors overpays by roughly an order of magnitude and delays the account fix by two years.
2. **[D] Cap the network at automation Level 1–2 (verification + mechanization, then autonomous mobile robots) for four of five sites.** Level 2 is modular, redeployable between buildings, and available on a robots-as-a-service basis — it is a bet on volume we can unwind. Level 3 (shuttle/ASRS goods-to-person) is a ten-year immovable bet on one building and is deferred to a separate Gate 3 decision.
3. **[D] Pilot at Site 2 (urban, high-turnover, representative order profile, medium lease), not Site 1 (largest, single-employer town).** This is derived from the scorecard in §5, not asserted from sentiment.
4. **[D] Commit in writing, before any equipment order, to no involuntary separation of any employee with ≥2 years' tenure for the duration of the program.** The network's 35% turnover makes this affordable. It is also the single cheapest insurance policy against becoming the next national news story — and against losing the exception-handling knowledge we need most during cutover.
5. **[D] Fund in tranches with named kill criteria.** Tranche 1 (Gate 0 + Track A) is a small, mostly-expense commitment. No Level 2 capital is released until Track A has demonstrably fixed error rates and the Gate 0 diagnostic has replaced the assumptions in §13.

**Cost to core (the rule: every commitment states what it takes from the running business).** This roadmap consumes roughly 1.5–2.5 FTE of senior operations bandwidth continuously for 30 months, one full-time program director, and accepts a deliberate 8–15% throughput dip at each converting site for 6–10 weeks [R]. It defers any network footprint rationalization by at least 24 months. It also forgoes an estimated 12–20 months of labor savings versus an aggressive big-bang program [R] — that is the explicit price of not failing publicly.

---

## 2. Decision sought at this meeting

| # | Decision | Amount / commitment |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Authorize **Gate 0 diagnostic**, 90 days | $600k–$1.1m, expensed [R] |
| D2 | Authorize **Track A** (error elimination), all five sites, in parallel with D1 | $1.2m–$3.0m capex + $400k opex [R] |
| D3 | Approve the **workforce commitment** in §7.4 for public and internal release | No direct cost; constrains future options |
| D4 | Approve **governance**: benefit realization audited by Finance, baseline frozen pre-change, halt criteria in §11.4 | No direct cost |
| D5 | Note that **no automation capital is authorized today**; Level 2 pilot capital is a Gate 1 decision in ~Month 4 | — |

Not sought today: any Level 2 or Level 3 capital, any site closure, any headcount action.

---

## 3. The central reframe: two problems, two solutions

The vendor conversation has fused three symptoms into one purchase order. They do not share a solution.

| Symptom | Actual driver [R] | Cheapest effective fix | Capex order of magnitude | Time to effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Error rates damaging key accounts** | Absent or bypassed verification at pick and pack; poor slotting causing look-alike adjacency; untrained new hires in the first 90 days; no root-cause loop by account | Scan-verify enforcement, pick/put-to-light on top-error SKU families, weight-check at pack-out, slotting rebuild, pick-path discipline, mandatory hold-and-recheck for the five most exposed accounts | $10⁴–$10⁵ per site | **4–12 weeks** |
| **Rising labor cost per line** | Travel time (typically 50–65% of picker time in person-to-goods operations [R]), overtime to cover absence, rework | Level 2 AMRs; Level 1 mechanization; slotting and batching | $10⁶–$10⁷ per site | 12–24 months |
| **35% picker turnover** | Physical load, wage position, first-90-day failure, schedule rigidity — partly the *cause* of the error rate | Onboarding redesign, ergonomics, schedule flexibility, wage-position correction where warranted, plus automation reducing physical load | $10⁵ per site | 6–18 months |

**Consequence for sequence.** Track A (error elimination) runs **network-wide, immediately, and independently of the automation sequence**. It is not a phase of the automation program; it is a separate program with its own owner that must succeed before automation capital is released. If Track A fixes the errors — and it should — the automation business case narrows to labor cost alone, which is exactly the discipline we want when evaluating a seven-figure purchase.

**Second-order benefit:** Track A also produces the clean data (SKU velocity, cube, lines/order, error root cause, actual pick rates) without which any automation design is guesswork and any vendor throughput model is unfalsifiable.

---

## 4. The automation ladder — degree of automation, defined

We reject the automate/don't-automate binary. Degree is a choice on five rungs.

| Level | Content | Capex per site [R] | Labor effect [R] | Reversibility | Volume-risk exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Slotting, batching, pick-path, engineered labor standards, incentive redesign, onboarding | <$150k | 8–15% lines/hr | Fully reversible | None |
| **1** | Scan-verify, pick/put-to-light, weight-check, conveyor/sortation extension, powered carts, print-and-apply | $0.5–2.5m | 10–20% lines/hr, large error reduction | Mostly reversible; some fixed conveyor | Low |
| **2** | **AMRs, person-to-goods** — robot-assisted picking, zone routing, cart-follow | $1.5–5m, or RaaS at $1.5–3k/robot/month | 25–45% lines/hr | **High — robots redeploy between sites in weeks** | Low–moderate |
| **3** | **Goods-to-person shuttle / ASRS / tote-based AS-RS** | $15–45m+ | 50–70% lines/hr in the automated zone | **Near zero — immovable, 10-yr bet on that building and that volume** | High |
| **4** | Robotic piece-picking, autonomous truck loading | Pilot cost only | Site-specific | N/A | Research |

**[D] Network target end-state:** Levels 0–1 at all five sites. Level 2 at three sites. Level 3 at **at most one** site, decided at Gate 3 no earlier than Month 24. Level 4 as a single contained pilot cell, funded as R&D, with no capacity dependency.

**The reason is flexibility, not cost.** Our volume outlook five years out is [V] — unverified. Level 3 converts an uncertain volume forecast into a fixed cost and a fixed building. Level 2 keeps the option to move the asset to whichever site the volume actually shows up in. We are willing to accept a worse modelled return on Level 2 in exchange for a real option. If the Gate 0 diagnostic shows genuinely durable, high-density, stable volume at one site, Level 3 becomes defensible there — but only there, and only with a demonstrated Level 2 track record first.

---

## 5. Site sequencing — scorecard, then conclusion

### 5.1 Scorecard criteria and weights [D]

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Order profile fit (lines/order, units/line, velocity curve, cube) | 20% | Determines whether AMR/GTP economics exist at all |
| Peak:average ratio | 10% | High peaks favor flexible labor + AMR over fixed GTP |
| Building physics & remaining lease (floor flatness, clear height, power, fire suppression, racking permit path) | 15% | Frequently the hidden cost that breaks the payback |
| Labor market liquidity & current turnover | 15% | High turnover = attrition runway = no forced separations |
| Key-account concentration served | 15% | Concentration = service risk during cutover = do not go first |
| Union / works-council / CBA status | 10% | Drives consultation timing, therefore sequence |
| Community exposure (share of town employment) | 15% | Drives reputational and political consequence of error |

### 5.2 Illustrative scores [R] — to be replaced at Gate 0

| | Profile fit | Peak:avg | Building | Labor liquidity | Account conc. | Labor relations | Community exposure | **Pilot suitability** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Site 1** — largest (~35–40% of network lines), owned, single-employer town, tenure-heavy, turnover est. **12–18%** | High | Low | Good | **Very low** | High | Non-union, high tenure | **Extreme** | **Lowest** |
| **Site 2** — urban, leased ~6 yrs remaining, turnover est. **45–55%**, order profile close to network median | High | Medium | Adequate | High | Medium | Non-union | Low | **Highest** |
| **Site 3** — mid-size, serves two of the five most error-exposed accounts, older building, low clear height | Medium | Medium | Poor for L3 | Medium | **Very high** | Non-union | Low | Medium (2nd) |
| **Site 4** — mid-size, strongly seasonal, short lease | Medium | **Very high** | Marginal | Medium | Low | Union / CBA [V] | Medium | Medium (3rd) |
| **Site 5** — smallest, pallet/case-heavy profile | **Low** | Low | n/a | Medium | Low | Non-union | Medium | Not a candidate |

### 5.3 Conclusions derived from the scorecard

- **Site 2 is the pilot.** It scores highest on the three criteria that matter for a first conversion: profile fit (so the result is technically meaningful), labor liquidity and high turnover (so headcount reduction lands entirely on attrition), and low community and account exposure (so a bad quarter is survivable). Its lease has enough term to amortize Level 2 but not Level 3 — which is the correct constraint for a pilot.
- **Site 1 is not the pilot, and its low turnover is the reason — not its politics.** At an estimated 12–18% turnover, Site 1 has roughly *one-third* of the annual attrition runway per employee that Site 2 has. Any given percentage headcount reduction there takes two to three times as long to absorb without forced separations. The community-employment fact makes an error there expensive; the attrition arithmetic makes it *slow*. Both point the same way. Site 1 is sequenced last, its automation is Level 1–2 only unless Gate 3 clears, and its reduction target is deliberately stretched over 4+ years (§7.3).
- **Transferability check — the opposite error.** A pilot at a site so atypical that success teaches nothing is as bad as a pilot that fails. Site 2 is chosen partly because its order profile sits near the network median [V — confirm at Gate 0]. If diagnostics show Site 2's profile is an outlier, the pilot moves to Site 3 and we accept the higher account-concentration risk with a heavier parallel-run overlay. This is a pre-stated flip.
- **Site 5 is a Level 0–1 site only.** Its case-and-pallet profile does not support piece-pick automation. It is also the site that forces the network question in §12.

### 5.4 Sequence

| Phase | Months | Site 1 | Site 2 | Site 3 | Site 4 | Site 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Track A + Level 0** | 0–7 | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ (first) | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Level 1** | 4–14 | ✔ | ✔ (with pilot) | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Level 2 pilot** | 6–18 | — | ✔ **pilot** | — | — | — |
| **Level 2 replicate** | 18–30 | — | expand | ✔ | ✔ | — |
| **Level 2 at Site 1** | 24–38 | ✔ | — | — | — | — |
| **Gate 3: Level 3 decision** | 24–30 | candidate | candidate (lease-limited) | no | no | no |
| **Level 4 pilot cell** | 20–32 | — | ✔ (contained) | — | — | — |

---

## 6. Gates and what each one buys

**Gate 0 — Diagnostic (Months 0–3). Authorized today.**
Deliverables: 12 months of line-level order data per site profiled (lines/order, units/line, cube, velocity ABC, seasonality, design-day vs. P95 day); error root-cause study by account; actual observed pick rates by zone; building surveys (floor flatness, clear height, power, sprinkler, permit path); labor market and turnover analysis per site; legal review (§7.5); baseline freeze. **Exit test:** we can state, with our own data, the labor cost per line and the DPMO per account at every site.

**Gate 1 — Level 2 pilot authorization (~Month 4).** Requires Gate 0 exit test passed, Track A showing ≥40% DPMO reduction trend at the first two sites, three competitively bid Level 2 designs with contractual throughput guarantees against *our* order profile, and a signed workforce commitment.

**Gate 2 — Replication authorization (~Month 18).** Requires the pilot to hold the §11.4

## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.

# Critique — Warehouse Automation & Workforce Transition Roadmap

## 1. Threshold finding: there is no output to review

The previous step returned nothing. No roadmap, no partial draft, no outline, no clarifying questions. Every one of the four deliverables the request explicitly names — (a) degree and sequence of automation per site, (b) redeploy/retrain/reduce plan, (c) service-level maintenance during conversion, (d) benefit-realization measurement — is absent.

This is a hard fail, not a "needs polish." The remainder of this review is therefore a specification for the next attempt rather than a line critique.

## 2. Unresolved framing question that must be answered before drafting

The only prior material is a v2.0 board paper on textile market entry — a different company, sector and problem. The next agent must decide and state, in one line, whether:

- **(a)** this is the same house style applied to a new decision (in which case inherit the conventions: `[V]/[R]/[D]` tagging, the "every commitment carries a stated cost to the core" rule, Gate 0 / Gate 1 structure, pre-stated flip criteria, explicit non-asserted load-bearing claims), or
- **(b)** this is an unrelated engagement.

Do **not** silently carry over content from the textile paper (Japan, Vietnam, rules of origin). Carrying over the *conventions* is defensible and probably desirable; carrying over the *substance* would be a serious error. Say which you are doing.

## 3. The analytical moves the deliverable must make (and that weak versions will miss)

**3.1 Separate the two problems the way the prior paper separated demand and supply.** Rising labor cost and unacceptable error rates are *different problems with different cheapest solutions*. Error rates are frequently fixed by scan-verify, pick-to-light, weight-check at pack-out, slotting, and pick-path discipline — capex in the tens of thousands, deployable in weeks. Labor cost reduction is the case for capital automation. A roadmap that solves errors *by buying goods-to-person* has overpaid by an order of magnitude and delayed the account-damage fix by two years. Fix errors first, network-wide, and independently of the automation sequence. If the draft does not make this split, it has missed the central insight.

- **Retention of the people you are about to make redundant.** Long-tenured pickers are the exception-handling knowledge base and are most needed *during* cutover. Stay-bonuses and a written no-forced-separation-before-stabilization commitment are cheaper than a failed go-live.
- **Network-level option.** Five sites with automation capex on the table raises the question the request does not ask but a good adviser does: should the network still be five sites? Address it briefly, even if only to defer it.
- **Maintenance and controls capability.** Automation converts picker headcount into technician headcount — a scarcer, more expensive labor pool. This is both a cost line and a *redeployment path* (the best retraining offer available).
- **Capital tranching.** "Capital is available but not unlimited" means the answer must be a gated funding request with a named first tranche and named kill criteria, not a total program number.

## 5. Measurement section — the usual failure mode

Do not propose "productivity" or "ROI" as the metric. Specify: cost per line and total cost-to-serve by site (the only figures that can prove the business case); lines/labor-hour at peak, not average; error rate as DPMO segmented by root cause and by key account; on-time ship and fill rate against pre-conversion baseline; realized throughput vs. modelled at design day; capex and schedule vs. plan; attrition-vs-plan. Two governance requirements: a **baseline frozen before any change**, and benefit realization audited by finance, not self-reported by the project team. State in advance the results that would halt or reverse the program.

## 6. Form

Board-legible, decision-shaped: an up-front recommendation, an explicit decision sought, per-site sequence table, phased timeline with gates, workforce numbers by site and by year, funding tranches, and a named risk register. Where data is absent (it entirely is — no volumes, no headcount, no site profiles), state assumptions in a visible register with tags and list the diagnostic data required before Gate 1. Do not invent precision.

## 1. Recommendation

**Do not buy the vendor's proposal. Split the problem in two, fix the account-damaging errors immediately with near-zero capital, and buy automation slowly, in a modular form, at the sites where it is cheapest to be wrong.**

Specifically:

1. **[D] Treat error rates and labor cost as two separate problems with two separate solutions.** Error rates are a process-and-verification problem solvable network-wide in 4–7 months for low single-digit millions or less [R]. Labor cost is the only legitimate case for capital automation. Buying goods-to-person to fix errors overpays by roughly an order of magnitude and delays the account fix by two years.
2. **[D] Cap the network at automation Level 1–2 (verification + mechanization, then autonomous mobile robots) for four of five sites.** Level 2 is modular, redeployable between buildings, and available on a robots-as-a-service basis — it is a bet on volume we can unwind. 3. **[D] Pilot at Site 2 (urban, high-turnover, representative order profile, medium lease), not Site 1 (largest, single-employer town).** This is derived from the scorecard in §5, not asserted from sentiment.
4. **[D] Commit in writing, before any equipment order, to no involuntary separation of any employee with ≥2 years' tenure for the duration of the program.** The network's 35% turnover makes this affordable. 5. **[D] Fund in tranches with named kill criteria.** Tranche 1 (Gate 0 + Track A) is a small, mostly-expense commitment. No Level 2 capital is released until Track A has demonstrably fixed error rates and the Gate 0 diagnostic has replaced the assumptions in §13.

## 3. The central reframe: two problems, two solutions

The vendor conversation has fused three symptoms into one purchase order. They do not share a solution.

| Symptom | Actual driver [R] | Cheapest effective fix | Capex order of magnitude | Time to effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Error rates damaging key accounts** | Absent or bypassed verification at pick and pack; poor slotting causing look-alike adjacency; untrained new hires in the first 90 days; no root-cause loop by account | Scan-verify enforcement, pick/put-to-light on top-error SKU families, weight-check at pack-out, slotting rebuild, pick-path discipline, mandatory hold-and-recheck for the five most exposed accounts | $10⁴–$10⁵ per site | **4–12 weeks** |
| **Rising labor cost per line** | Travel time (typically 50–65% of picker time in person-to-goods operations [R]), overtime to cover absence, rework | Level 2 AMRs; Level 1 mechanization; slotting and batching | $10⁶–$10⁷ per site | 12–24 months |
| **35% picker turnover** | Physical load, wage position, first-90-day failure, schedule rigidity — partly the *cause* of the error rate | Onboarding redesign, ergonomics, schedule flexibility, wage-position correction where warranted, plus automation reducing physical load | $10⁵ per site | 6–18 months |

**Consequence for sequence.** Track A (error elimination) runs **network-wide, immediately, and independently of the automation sequence**. It is not a phase of the automation program; it is a separate program with its own owner that must succeed before automation capital is released. If Track A fixes the errors — and it should — the automation business case narrows to labor cost alone, which is exactly the discipline we want when evaluating a seven-figure purchase.

**Second-order benefit:** Track A also produces the clean data (SKU velocity, cube, lines/order, error root cause, actual pick rates) without which any automation design is guesswork and any vendor throughput model is unfalsifiable.

## 4. The automation ladder — degree of automation, defined

We reject the automate/don't-automate binary. Degree is a choice on five rungs.

| Level | Content | Capex per site [R] | Labor effect [R] | Reversibility | Volume-risk exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Slotting, batching, pick-path, engineered labor standards, incentive redesign, onboarding | <$150k | 8–15% lines/hr | Fully reversible | None |
| **1** | Scan-verify, pick/put-to-light, weight-check, conveyor/sortation extension, powered carts, print-and-apply | $0.5–2.5m | 10–20% lines/hr, large error reduction | Mostly reversible; some fixed conveyor | Low |
| **2** | **AMRs, person-to-goods** — robot-assisted picking, zone routing, cart-follow | $1.5–5m, or RaaS at $1.5–3k/robot/month | 25–45% lines/hr | **High — robots redeploy between sites in weeks** | Low–moderate |
| **3** | **Goods-to-person shuttle / ASRS / tote-based AS-RS** | $15–45m+ | 50–70% lines/hr in the automated zone | **Near zero — immovable, 10-yr bet on that building and that volume** | High |
| **4** | Robotic piece-picking, autonomous truck loading | Pilot cost only | Site-specific | N/A | Research |

**[D] Network target end-state:** Levels 0–1 at all five sites. Level 2 at three sites. Level 3 at **at most one** site, decided at Gate 3 no earlier than Month 24. Level 4 as a single contained pilot cell, funded as R&D, with no capacity dependency.

**The reason is flexibility, not cost.** Our volume outlook five years out is [V] — unverified. Level 3 converts an uncertain volume forecast into a fixed cost and a fixed building. Level 2 keeps the option to move the asset to whichever site the volume actually shows up in. We are willing to accept a worse modelled return on Level 2 in exchange for a real option. If the Gate 0 diagnostic shows genuinely durable, high-density, stable volume at one site, Level 3 becomes defensible there — but only there, and only with a demonstrated Level 2 track record first.
